source: IdeaGauge, the Business Idea Evaluator by Derick van Vuren (takeacourse.online), built on The Startup Blueprint (2nd ed., 2025). Generated from the app's own criteria model.
scale: 0 to 100 per criterion; 0 is bad or low, 100 is good or high. Every criterion is worded so that higher is better.

biz.title: Business Analysis
biz.sub: How strong is the opportunity itself?

me.title: Personal Fit
me.sub: The idea matters, but so does the founder. Be honest.

own.title: Your Own Criteria
own.sub: Your goals, your rules. Adjust the defaults or add what matters to you.

criteria.help: Newer = higher score. Novelty helps, but execution beats novelty. That's why this weighs ×1.

criteria.q: Does it do things in a more valuable way?
criteria.help: Even old ideas win when they deliver clearly more value than what exists today.
Painkillers beat vitamins. The #1 startup killer is building something nobody needs.
Delight drives word-of-mouth and retention.
Can a customer state the benefit in one sentence?

criteria.q: Can I have a competitive advantage?
criteria.help: Your unfair advantage: distribution, technology, brand, cost, or insight.
More crowded = lower score. Some competition validates demand; a stampede kills margins.

criteria.q: Does it have better value than rivals?
criteria.help: Why would anyone switch to you? Better, cheaper, faster, or nicer. Pick at least one.
Rarer = higher score. Rarity supports pricing power.
Easily copied = lower score. Think patents, network effects, switching costs, know-how.
Easily substituted = lower score. What else solves the same job for your customer?
Needs survive recessions; wants don't. Must-have beats nice-to-have.
Can revenue grow much faster than costs and headcount?
Simple businesses launch faster and break less.
Do you know exactly who buys, and can you find more of them repeatably?
Subscriptions and repeat purchases score high; one-off project income scores low.
Is the market big enough to reach your goals? Small ponds cap big dreams.

criteria.q: Does it have a low entry barrier?
criteria.help: Low barrier = lower score: if it's easy for you to enter, it's easy for everyone.
Blue = uncontested new market space (high score). Red = bloody feature wars (low score).
Effectuation = starting from the means you already have: who you are, what you know, who you know.
A great idea that fights your nature will exhaust you.
You'll spend thousands of hours here. Interest is fuel.

criteria.q: Do I have passion for this?
criteria.help: Passion is what survives the third bad month. Investors and customers can feel it.
Domain expertise shortens your learning curve dramatically.
Market, customer and industry knowledge. Do you know this world?
If you lack expertise today, how fast can you learn it or hire it?

criteria.q: Can I network in this field?
criteria.help: Networks bring first customers, advice, and talent.
Ideas are worthless without execution. Be brutally honest here.

criteria.q: Do I have the needed resources?
criteria.help: Money, time, tools, people. Underfunding is a top-3 startup killer.
The gut check: when you explain it, do people immediately get it?

criteria.q: Can I potentially achieve my goals?
criteria.help: Does this idea actually lead to the life and outcomes you want?

criteria.q: What is the probability of failure?
criteria.help: Low probability of failure = high score. Consider the risks you can't control.

criteria.q: Do I have support from family/friends?
criteria.help: The journey is hard; support systems keep founders going.
Does this business give you the lifestyle and autonomy you want?
Memberships create recurring revenue and community.
Meaning sustains motivation long after novelty fades.

own_examples: Do you have personal freedom? (the lifestyle and autonomy you want)
Is it membership based? (recurring revenue and a community)
Can I run it from home or online?
Does it fit my family schedule?
Can I start it with little money?
Does it use the skills I already have?
Could I sell the business one day?
Is it good for the environment or my community?
Can I work with people I like?
Is it close to where I live?
Will I still enjoy it in ten years?

novel: Whether others already sell this. New is a plus, but execution matters more than novelty.
advantage: Your unfair edge over rivals: lower cost, better technology, a brand, a network, or insight others lack.
crowded: How many competitors already sell to the same customers. Some competition proves demand; too much kills margins.
rare: How hard it is to find something like this. Rarity supports higher prices.
noCopy: How hard it is for a rival to copy you, thanks to patents, know-how, contracts, a network or switching costs. Often called a moat.
noSub: A substitute is a different way to get the same job done (for a taxi: walking, a bus, a bicycle). Fewer substitutes is better.
scalable: Revenue can grow much faster than costs and staff. Software scales; a one-person service usually does not.
simple: Easy to explain, build and run. Simple businesses launch faster and break less.
custBase: You know exactly who buys, and you can find more of them again and again.
revenue: Money that comes in regularly: subscriptions, retainers, repeat orders. One-off projects are unpredictable.
income: How big the business can get: whether the market is large enough for your goals.
barrier: What it takes to start this kind of business: money, licenses, skills. A low barrier is easy for you, but also for every competitor, so it scores low.
ocean: A red ocean is an existing market full of competitors fighting on price. A blue ocean is new, uncontested market space where you set the rules. Blue scores high.
effect: Starting from what you already have (who you are, what you know, who you know) instead of waiting for the perfect plan or big funding.
expertise: Hands-on skill at doing the work itself.
knowledge: Understanding of the market, the customers and the industry.
acquire: If you lack a skill today, how fast you could learn it or hire someone who has it.
obvious: The gut check: when you explain the idea, people get it at once and say 'why doesn't this exist already?'
failure: How likely the business is to fail, counting the risks you cannot control. A LOW chance of failure gets a HIGH score.
